query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: When subjected to mechanical loading in a corrosive environment, a high‐entropy alloy that is microstructurally tailored (via low-level microalloying that promotes grain refinement and controlled secondary phase dispersion) will dynamically form an ultra‐nanocrystalline or near‐amorphous surface layer that rapidly re‐passivates. This surface layer acts simultaneously to blunt wear by resisting plastic deformation and to reduce corrosion by sustaining a continuous, self-healing passive film.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy alloy (for example, an AlCoCrFeNiMo-based alloy) with a dual‐phase or coarse microstructure that is capable of transforming its top layer under mechanical shear.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small amount of microalloying element (such as B or Si) to pre-refine the grain structure and promote controlled secondary phase precipitation, thereby predisposing the alloy to develop an ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous surface layer under wear loading.
generation.conditions: Test samples under (a) wear-only conditions in an inert or non-corrosive environment and (b) combined wear-corrosion conditions (e.g., under a 3.5 wt.% NaCl electrolyte) with identical mechanical loads, ensuring that the operating shear conditions are sufficient to activate dynamic surface layer formation.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of an ultra‐nanocrystalline or near‐amorphous surface layer that supports rapid re-passivation by offering high-density grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: During mechanical loading, the enhanced microalloyed HEA undergoes dynamic amorphization or severe grain refinement at its surface. The resultant refined layer increases the diffusion of oxygen and other passivating species, enabling the rapid repair and stabilization of the passive oxide film. This simultaneously curtails plastic deformation (reducing wear) and limits corrosive attack (reducing corrosion).
generation.predicted_outcome: In the combined wear-corrosion tests, the microalloyed (tailored) HEA will exhibit lower wear rates, reduced friction, more stable open-circuit potentials during mechanical cycling, and lower corrosion current densities compared to the baseline alloy. The synergistic improvement should be greater than the sum of improvements observed in isolated wear or corrosion tests.
generation.baseline: An otherwise identical HEA without the microalloying addition—i.e., presenting a coarser initial microstructure that does not readily form the dynamic ultra-nanocrystalline layer under mechanical stress.
generation.boundary: The predicted benefits will manifest when the testing environment provides sufficient mechanical shear to induce the dynamic surface transformation and allows rapid passivation. In environments that are overly oxidizing or where the imposed mechanical stresses are too low to trigger the transformation, this mechanism may not be active, and the differences between the tailored and baseline alloys may become negligible.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on the findings from the dynamic amorphization and inverse Hall–Petch behavior observed in CoCrFeMnNi alloys (PMC7311485::web::012::results_and_discussion) and on the microstructural refinement and passive film stabilization effects due to low-level B addition in AlCoCrFeNiMoTi alloys (PMC12565319::web::000::abstract). The new extension is the coupling of these effects in a simultaneous wear-corrosion environment. There is uncertainty regarding how the aggressive, corrosive mechanical environment might influence the kinetics and stability of the dynamically formed surface layer.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA coatings on identical substrates: one set with a microalloying addition (B or Si) engineered to induce pre-refined microstructure and dynamic surface layer formation, and a matched baseline coating without the addition. Subject both sets to (i) wear-only testing (e.g., using a tribometer in an inert atmosphere) and (ii) combined wear-corrosion testing (e.g., sliding under a controlled load in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution).
measurements: Wear rates and friction coefficients (using profilometry and friction monitoring)
Electrochemical parameters such as corrosion current density and OCP stability (via potentiodynamic polarization and real-time OCP monitoring)
Post-test surface characterization (using SEM and TEM) to verify the presence and integrity of the ultra-nanocrystalline/near-amorphous surface layer and passivation film
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the microalloyed (tailored) HEA does not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in both reduced wear rates and enhanced corrosion resistance (i.e., similar friction behavior, corrosion current density, and OCP stability) relative to the baseline under combined wear-corrosion conditions, or if detailed surface analyses fail to reveal the formation of the dynamic ultra-nanocrystalline/amorphous layer that is purported to mediate the dual protection.

cited_evidence.text: To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. Boron incorporation improves the coating’s microhardness and wear resistance, with the highest wear resistance achieved at x = 1, where abrasive and oxidative wear predominate. This work studied an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy that was manufactured using a laser-based consolidation additive manufacturing process. We showed that low friction and high wear resistance are achievable with bare high entropy alloys in inert environments. These characteristics are linked to the shear-induced formation of a highly refined, near-amorphous surface film that exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior. The detrimental role of environments, specifically those that result in oxidation, was mitigated by tribological testing in a UHV environment. A newly proposed amorphization model was used to accurately predict the grain size-dependent shear strength, and thus friction coefficient.

AbstractGeothermal process equipment and accessories are usually manufactured from low-alloy steels which offer affordability but increase the susceptibility of the materials to corrosion. Applying erosion-corrosion-resistant coatings to these components could represent an economical solution to the problem. In this work, testing of two newly developed laser metal deposited high-entropy alloy (LMD-HEA) coatings—CoCrFeNiMo0.85 and Al0.5CoCrFeNi, applied to carbon and stainless steels—was carried out at the Hellisheidi geothermal power plant. Tests in three different geothermal environments were performed at the Hellisheidi site: wellhead test at 194 °C and 14 bar, erosion test at 198 °C and 15 bar, and aerated test at 90 °C and 1 bar. Post-test microstructural characterization was performed via Scanning Eletron Microscope (SEM), Back-Scattered Electrons analysis (BSE), Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS), optical microscopy, and optical profilometry while erosion assessment was carried out using an image and chemical analysis.
